A study was conducted to characterize the plasma produced by the IShTAR plasma source, which is a helicon-based device, in preparation for testing RF heating in the ISTT-1B tokamak. To ensure accurate operation, it was essential to understand how the plasma reacts to power and gas, which was achieved through comprehensive measurements of plasma parameters using a range of diagnostic tools. These findings were incorporated into a computer model that simulates the plasma behavior and has been utilized for designing successful experiments. The research revealed that the plasma source can produce high densities and temperatures at relatively low powers, although it was found that increasing the power above a certain point results in plasma degradation. A simulation model was also developed to evaluate the possibility of using the IShTAR source in a combined helicon and ECRH configuration.

While gold-standard nuclear segmentation for histopathology images is highly regarded for
diagnostic accuracy, it is exceptionally time-consuming to accomplish, with top experts
spending multiple days completing a single case study. To streamline this process, a
automated technology known as W-Net has been created, allowing users to quickly and
effortlessly mark individual cancer cells within suspicious regions, without requiring
advanced computational powers. Based on a two-stage convolutional network, W-Net facilitates
user-guided correction of existing predictions, effectively incorporating valuable user
feedback into the model. Through testing on multiple datasets, W-Net has demonstrated
superior performance in multiple metrics, with notable improvements in segmentation
accuracy, score, and map when compared to alternative methods. Moreover, W-Net exhibits
robustness in handling complex, multi-class datasets, including those featuring diverse
cellular patterns and mixed cell types.

Let's consider a non-Abelian group G that acts on a set Omega in a certain way, without any assumption of finiteness or stability properties. For any subset omega of Omega, we define the space V_omega by taking the vector spanning the set omega, which we can do since the characteristic isn't 2. Then, we can identify a subgroup of G corresponding to omega, denoted as S_Omega or S_sp(omega) for the special orthogonal or symplectic group, depending on the action of G on the vector V_omega. This paper explores the properties of these subgroups under the action of G on Omega, without any requirement for stability, and confirms the exchange property for parts of the action, in addition to establishing the equivalence of certain double cosets.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are then depicted as non-linear partial differential equations. The soliton and black hole solutions are examined to determine their stability and temperature, with observations made on how external fields affect them. The soliton solutions are found to be independent of coordinates and consistently maintain a constant temperature across all parameter variations. In contrast, black hole solutions are found to vary based on coordinates and exhibit temperature fluctuations when certain parameters are altered. The model's stability is also shown to be influenced by the cosmological constant, with the soliton solutions becoming unstable under certain conditions, while the black hole solutions exhibit hairy features when a specific field is applied.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Despite its advantages, the medical application of elastography is limited due to poor image quality resulting from inadequate tissue sampling, especially in ultrasound elastography. Developing accurate models to predict the behavior of tissues under external pressure can significantly enhance the imaging capability of elastography. Unfortunately, models based on partial differential equations require labor-intensive computational power and are often ineffective for real-time imaging. In contrast, model-based elastography using the analytic solution of the wave equation has been proven effective in ultrasound elastography. Nonetheless, these methods suffer from limited field-of-view (FOV) due to source and receiver array limitations, leading to the development of the virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique. VSSA further enhances imaging by accurately estimating the lateral shift of elastography images. This paper reviews the fundamentals of elastography, model-based elastography, synthetic aperture imaging, and VSSA, also discussing the challenges and limitations of each method. Furthermore, this paper details the development of VSSA and evaluates its performance in simulations and clinical trials. In particular, simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of VSSA in determining tissue biomechanical properties even with low degree of deformation. Moreover, clinical trials indicate that VSSA can accurately estimate the lateral shift of elastography images, resulting in the enhancement of imaging capability of ultrasound elastography.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

In the $k$-centers clustering problem, we divide data points into clusters based on their proximity to predetermined center points. This problem has various applications, particularly in identifying representative points in large datasets. For a dynamic $k$-centers problem with $n$ points in $d$ dimensions, we establish a approximate algorithm that yields a solution with a cluster center distance of $O(k^{1/4}\cdot d^{1/4}\cdot \log^{1/2}(n))$ from the optimal solution, using a data structure of size $O(k\cdot d\cdot \log(n))$. This result improves upon the previous state of the art for high-dimensional data, where the optimal solution has a cluster center distance of $O(k^{1/2}\cdot \log(n))$ from the previously known optimal solution.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games are first solved on a coarser state-based representation, which are then combined into a comprehensive'metagame' that accounts for all interactions between the scaled-down state categories. Each of these scaled games can be readily solved using existing local methods, such as value iteration. We connect the results of these scaled games to the overall metagame using a generalized linear learning process. This hierarchical structure enables the efficient handling of large-scale discrete stochastic evasion games by reducing computational expenses. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our hierarchical approach by applying it to a range of increasingly complex random grid worlds.

While the number of vector bosons exceeds one in many LHC experiments, the processes involving them are typically complex and difficult to calculate due to QED's high complexity. However, through a clever rearrangement of the fundamental principles, the likelihood of finding multiple vectors can be efficiently calculated from the probability of one vector being produced many times. This approach, known as the Vector Boson Approximation, simplifies calculations and makes them more manageable. Our research extends this concept to muon colliders and explores how the VBA affects the measurement of certain Higgs properties, particularly Higgs decay into two photons, by comparing the VBA's predictions to exact calculations.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to serious negative consequences, known as catastrophic
interference. To overcome this, we show that isolating sub-networks for each
task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields substantial improvements
in performance. We validate our approach by applying these methods to both
simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom scenarios.

We explore an interesting development where Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem leads to an unforeseen consequence - the completion of arithmetic with the standard peptide theory.  To arrive at this result, we establish a decision-making framework for peer reviewers within the standard peptide theory, which in turn requires a modified version of Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem.  This modified version is expressed in terms of the peptide theory itself, rather than its underlying arithmetic component.  One particular variant of the modified theorem is notable for its simplicity and is often referred to as the "Gathered Incompleteness Theorem".  The principles discussed here can be extended to other theories beyond arithmetic.

We investigate the function $f\in NV$ within Clifford analysis, where $NV$ denotes the space of functions that vanish at infinity, and $f$ satisfies the Dirac equation $Lf=0$. A key aspect of this research involves establishing that if $f$ meets these conditions and possesses three distinct points of inflection, then it must be a scalar multiple of the function $\text{cos}(x)$, when $f$ is assumed to be real-valued.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on minimizing the difference between the restored and true images, but also on selecting the most likely one. This phenomenon is reflected in the theory behind the regularized inverse problem, which involves finding the restored image by minimizing a cost function consisting of an accuracy term, representing the discrepancy between the restored and true images, and a prior constraint, aimed at ensuring the restored image complies with prior knowledge. Because the true image is actually what's being sought, the accuracy term is necessarily linked to the measurement process. This connection guides the development of a novel training strategy for Conditional GANs, which yields a generator capable of restoring the most likely image from noisy data. This model excels in various tasks such as image denoisation, deblurring and super-resolution, including challenging cases like phase recovery in MRI.

This article examines the existence of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems from a mathematical perspective. A key requirement for surfaces to be invariant involves the Lie derivative of the surface's equation being equal to zero. This process is applied to a specific surface equation, resulting in a new Lie derivative that describes the surface's properties. In the case of dynamical systems described by nonlinear partial differential equations, the article discusses the implications of these properties on the system's stability and invariants in both continuous and discrete time frameworks. Although the article focuses on surface invariants within dynamical systems, it also explores the relationship with other invariant concepts such as conservation laws, symmetries, and integrals.

The interstellar medium is capable of revealing its complex structure and regional variability through the pattern of scintillation on pulsar images. This variability can be studied systematically by observing the position and shape of scintillation patterns, which are influenced by the scattering of radio waves within the interstellar medium. We observed the pulsar B1133+16 over a period of seven years, and our data reveal that the pattern of scintillation on its image remains relatively stable, changing only slightly over time. This is an unusual finding, as similar research on other pulsars showed much greater variation. We were able to map the distance to the scintillation patterns as approximately 300 AU, which suggests that the pulsar is located near the solar system. Furthermore, we found that the Earth must pass through a region of enhanced turbulence on approximately annual basis, which indicates that this turbulence is likely associated with a large structure in the interstellar medium that extends over several solar system lengths.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through expanded convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked convolution neural networks, but its pitch control is restricted due to fixed filter weights. To overcome this limitation, we introduce pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural networks, incorporating previous outputs to adapt filter weights based on the input pitch, resulting in a larger number of parameters compared to traditional WaveNet. Quasi-periodic beta attenuation is also proposed to expand convolution neural networks in pitch-dependent WN, enabling efficient pitch control without sacrificing high-fidelity audio generation. Experimentally, QPNet outperforms WaveNet and its variants on MELD, MSSD, and FR scores, demonstrating superior quality and similarity in generated samples. The code for QPNet is available at https://github.com/NoeG/QPNet.

Bicategories incorporate extra structure beyond extensivity, extending the definition that applies to both categories and categories with composition. Specifically, defining bicategories uses the same graph-based method used for categories with composition, except that the graph's orientation matters. This added complexity leads to added complexity in their theories. To make progress in these complex theories, we introduce a new concept called the shadow bicategory, a companion to the marker bicategory that forms the basis for a duality principle. In effect, shadow bicategories serve as a bridge between the original marker bicategories, allowing us to recast the duality principle in bicategorical terms and ultimately derive the fundamental property that marks a bicategory as extending a category.

Deep neural networks depend on robust training data, and noisy input data can significantly impede their performance. This research focuses on investigating an essential but poorly understood aspect of deep neural network training: how networks are affected by spatially concentrated noise in their input data. Unlike traditional learning theory, which studies generalization skills in relation to model complexity and training data quality, considers little the effect of spatially localized noise. Using Gaussian neural networks as a theoretical framework and convolutional neural networks as real-world examples, our findings reveal that deep networks struggle drastically to generalize when trained with spatially concentrated noise, and even small amounts of such noise can severely impair performance. Even after completing training, the networks exhibit significant difficulties in ignoring noise in new input images, and this noise can be extremely challenging to differentiate from meaningful features using various statistical tests.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been propelled by the massive amount of data being generated and the importance of scaling to large graphs. Despite these achievements, several key challenges remain, including the substantial computational cost, memory requirements, and GNN model training difficulties, particularly in models using deformation capabilities. These issues stem from the complex and inefficient nature of traditional graph convolution operations. Building upon the fundamental concept of graph convolution, we present a novel type of graph convolution called the Lorentzian graph convolution, characterized by a precise analysis of its frequency response. This analysis reveals that Lorentzian graph convolutions operate under specific frequency rejection characteristics, allowing them to efficiently process small-scale local networks efficiently. We also introduce a simple yet effective GNN model called Lorentzian GNN (LGNN), incorporating Lorentzian graph convolutions, designed to tackle small-sized intrinsic networks. Our experiments show that LGNN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmark datasets, consistently delivering superior performance while significantly reducing training costs and memory consumption.

This research focuses on identifying an object within a wave equation, specifically an internal source generating sound waves inside a closed container, using measurements from the container's exterior. By reinterpreting the weak formulation of the wave equation and utilizing a specific observer location, we derive an operator that maps the object to be found to a known quantity. Subsequent application of a regularization method enables the recovery of the desired object, and a numerical example demonstrates the proposed technique's effectiveness.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

In this note, we explore a class of gravity theories, referred to as hefty gravity, which are parameterized by two gauge metrics derived from a fundamental scalar field interacting with a Weyl tensor. We demonstrate that both harmonic gauge conditions yield identical results and are equivalent, thus requiring only a single condition to specify a solution within this framework. Additionally, we discuss the implications of having two gauge metrics and show that they are connected through a conformally equivalent relationship. This connection provides an interesting perspective on the numerous harmonic gauge conditions and their inherent symmetry.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, thereby illustrating the underlying classical physics through which these states can be determined. This transformation exposes the structure of thermal equilibrium states within a representation that is both efficient for computing and visually clear, specifically through a depiction of the Weyl-Wigner operator phase space. A key transformation factor, which is itself a unitary operator, plays a crucial role in this structure, and its impact on the underlying classical physics must be taken into account when analyzing the properties of thermal equilibrium states.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the easiest $s$-channel susy model, we examine the possibility that the mass equilibrium condition is met with TeV-scale $CP$-even Higgs bosons and top-like light stop quarks. In this analysis, we set the top quark's decay into the light stop to dominate over the decay into the light Higgs boson. By incorporating the ease criterion and mass equivalence, we establish lower bounds on the stop mass and the minimal supersymmetric standard model's light Higgs boson mass. Furthermore, we find that the stop mass must exceed 900 GeV, and the light Higgs boson mass must exceed 107 GeV to avoid both the failure of electroweak symmetry breaking and the $CP$-even light Higgs boson's dominance over the $CP$-odd Higgs boson in fermiophobic decays. For completeness, we also consider the ease criterion and mass equivalence in the light of the light stop's decay into the light Higgs boson and the minimal supersymmetric standard model's dark matter component. In this case, we determine the stop mass must exceed 630 GeV to prevent the light stop from being completely decoupled from the light Higgs boson. We employ a spin-orbitally resolved tight-binding model to describe the electronic behavior of transition metal oxides. The model's validity is demonstrated for 4d and 5d $d^1$ and $d^2$ transition metal oxides with rocksalt structure through a comparison of its results to first-principles calculations and experimental data on energy spectra and effective one-electron weights. The model's sensitivity to geometric distortions is illustrated using a $[110]$ tilt boundary model. The interplay of $t_{2g}$ and $eg$ $d$-orbital characters is analyzed and the role of spin-orbit interaction in defining the $t_{2g}$ or $eg$ symmetry of electrons is emphasized.

This research focuses on the relative quantum geometric quantization in the context of algebraic geometry, specifically for symplectic reductions defined by ample line bundles. It is shown that for a particular type of birational transformation called toric symplectic reductions, the associated data, including the underlying geometry and mathematical structure, remain unchanged at their equivalence class when viewed from a certain perspective. This implies that the associated invariants, such as the Weyl group, remain the same under this type of transformation. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that these invariants can be used to retrieve the original data and mathematical structure at their equivalence class when viewed from the same perspective.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in medical imaging is being explored where an additional component that produces a probability prediction is added to the standard GAN structure. This model produces a more accurate representation of new data points that resemble the original distribution. To test this concept, a simple GAN was created to edit chest X-rays by removing the background. However, there are issues with training such a complex model using limited data sets, particularly when labeling is time-consuming and costly. To mitigate this challenge, a self-supervised approach was developed where the model was trained to recreate the image without a learning curve, and significant improvements were seen in editing results when re-training the model on individual patients. This research demonstrates the versatility of GANs in complex tasks such as image segmentation and verifies the findings through a simple evaluation metric. To apply this model in a practical setting, further work is required, particularly in evaluating the long-term effectiveness of this model in editing new data points from unknown distributions.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool enables users to easily visualize high-dimensional data through embedding techniques such as PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, and others, and to interact with these visualizations in various ways. With ViDaExpert, users can derive and visualize clustering structures from their data using different methods, including automated and interactive tools. The application also offers a range of features for data preprocessing, quality control, and outlier detection. Furthermore, ViDaExpert provides a text analysis module for handling text-based data, including topic modeling and word embeddings. The application is designed to be highly intuitive and easy to use, with a graphical interface that allows users to navigate and customize visualizations and analyses through a simple and intuitive interface.
